court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: A boarding-house keeper's statutory lien on a boarder's furniture for unpaid board takes priority over an unrecorded chattel mortgage predating the debt, and the keeper need not specifically invoke the lien at the moment she refuses to surrender the goods to preserve it.

quotes.text: It follows, therefore, that the justice was right in giving judgment in favor of the defendant, Cushing, under her lien as a boarding house keeper.

The chattel mortgage given the plaintiff by the defendant, Green, not having been recorded until after all the indebtedness claimed by the defendant, Cushing, in this action accrued, was not a valid lien upon the furniture as against the defendant Cushing’s claim under the boarding house keeper’s act.

This being a statutory lien, we do not think it was necessary for her so to do at that time, especially as she did not give any other reason or special ground why she refused to deliver the property to the plaintiff.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: A husband and wife who agreed to jointly furnish a boarder with board, lodging, and use of a room -- the wife supplying the house and the husband the provisions, sharing proceeds equally -- validly created a joint debt owed to them both, since a husband may lawfully agree that his wife receive compensation for her own services and property.

quotes.text: The defendants set up as a counterclaim in this action a demand against the plaintiff for board, lodging and use of room, which were supplied and furnished to the plaintiff by the defendants jointly.

We think under the circumstances disclosed the defendants had a right and could legally make a contract by which the wife should receive a share of the proceeds of such board and use of room, for the use of her house and for her services, and that such contract having been made, and the plaintiff having promised to pay the defendants jointly for such board and use of room, with full knowledge of the agreement between the defendants, she cannot now insist that her debt was to the husband alone, and thus defeat the defendants’ counterclaim.
But even under such circumstances the husband might covenant and agree that his wife should receive pay for her services on her own account.

notes: No specific duration of plaintiff's occupancy is stated in the facts.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: A boarding-house keeper is not an insurer of a boarder's goods as an innkeeper would be; rather, as bailee for mutual benefit she is liable for a patron's stolen property only upon proof she failed to exercise ordinary care, a burden plaintiff did not carry.

quotes.text: A boarder is not a guest in the sense in which it is applied with reference to an innkeeper’s liability (Hancock v. Rand, 94 N. Y. 1; 46 Am. Rep. 112); and unlike the latter, who is liable as an insurer of his patron’s goods (Hulett v. Swift, 33 N. Y. 571), a boarding-house keeper is answerable for a loss of the goods only if he has omitted to exercise ordinary care to prevent it.
A boarding-house keeper, furthermore, is in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, in contemplation of law a custodian of his patron’s goods.
The judgment should be reversed and a new trial granted, With costs to appellant to abide the event.

notes: No specific length of the boarders' stay is given in the facts.
